title: NHS & private dentistry: funding and ethics
blurb: NHS charge bands in England and what each covers, who is exempt, private fees, capitation plans and insurance, and the ethics of offering private options.
question: A 62-year-old NHS patient needs two fillings and a crown. She asks whether she'll have to pay, which band this falls into, and whether she 'has to go private' for a white filling on a back tooth. How would the team answer her accurately and ethically?

teach.h: Two ways to pay, one standard of care
teach.body: UK patients can have NHS dental care, which is state-funded with patient charges unless they are exempt, or private care, which they pay for directly or through a plan or insurance. Many practices offer both. Whichever route, GDC standards are the same: put patients' interests first, give clear information about options and costs, and get valid consent. In England, NHS dentistry is commissioned locally by Integrated Care Boards (ICBs), and NHS dentists are paid through contracts measured in units of dental activity (UDAs).

levels.label: Band 3
levels.sub: + crowns, bridges, dentures, other lab work

levels.label: Band 1
levels.sub: Exam, diagnosis, X-rays, advice, scale and polish if needed, fluoride varnish or sealants

teach.caption: Each band includes everything in the bands below it. The patient pays one charge per course of treatment, for the highest band needed. Urgent NHS care (such as pain relief or a temporary filling) is charged at the Band 1 rate. Charge amounts change each April, so always check the current figures.

teach.h: Who is exempt from NHS dental charges in England?
head: Patient
Pays NHS charges?
rows: Pregnant, or had a baby in the last 12 months
Aged 60 or over, with no other exemption
teach.caption: Qualifying benefits include Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Pension Credit Guarantee Credit and, with conditions, Universal Credit. Patients claiming an exemption are asked for evidence, and false claims can lead to a penalty charge. Rules differ elsewhere: for example, NHS check-ups are free for everyone in Scotland, and in Wales for under-25s and over-60s.

teach.text: Over-60s get free NHS prescriptions in England, but NOT free NHS dental treatment. Age alone is not an exemption for adults; only under-18s (or under-19s in full-time education) are exempt on age.

teach.caption: Simpler maintenance plans cover only check-ups and hygiene visits; fuller capitation plans may also include some treatment. Patients should always know what is and isn't covered.

steps.label: Options
steps.sub: NHS, private, or no treatment, with pros and cons

steps.label: Written plan and costs
steps.sub: Clear about what is NHS and what is private

steps.label: Update if it changes
steps.sub: New plan and estimate before going ahead

teach.caption: The GDC expects patients to get a written treatment plan and cost estimate before treatment starts. In England, NHS plans for Band 2 and 3 courses use the form FP17DC.

teach.h: The ethics of offering private options
teach.body: Patients can choose private treatment for part of an NHS course, such as a tooth-coloured filling on a back tooth for appearance, but they must be told clearly what is available on the NHS and what is private. It is wrong to suggest clinically necessary treatment is only available privately, to pressure a patient, or to put the practice's income before their interests. As a nurse, never push products or treatments for profit. If you see patients being misled, that is a concern to raise.

items: Band 1: exam, X-rays, advice, scale and polish if needed, prevention. Band 2: + fillings, RCT, extractions. Band 3: + crowns, bridges, dentures.
One charge per course, at the highest band needed; urgent care is charged at the Band 1 rate.
Exempt: under 18, under 19 in full-time education, pregnant or baby in last 12 months, qualifying benefits, HC2.
Private: fee per item, capitation or maintenance plans, or insurance.
Always a written plan and cost estimate; be clear what is NHS and what is private; never pressure.

summary: You can now explain what each NHS charge band in England covers, identify who is exempt from charges, describe private fee-per-item care, capitation plans and insurance, and explain the ethical rules around treatment plans, costs and offering private options.

A.q: A patient asks how much her treatment will cost before agreeing to it. What must she be given?
options: A verbal estimate at the next visit
A written treatment plan and cost estimate
A copy of the practice's full private price list
An invoice once treatment is complete
A.why: The GDC expects patients to receive a written treatment plan with a cost estimate before treatment starts, so they can make an informed choice.

whyNot.0: Costs need to be given in writing, and before treatment, not later.
whyNot.2: A price list is useful but isn't a personal plan showing what she will pay.
whyNot.3: An invoice after treatment comes too late for informed consent.

A.q: An NHS patient in England needs a root canal treatment and an extraction. Which band applies?
A.why: Root canal treatment and extractions are Band 2 treatments, which also include everything in Band 1.

whyNot.0: Band 1 covers examination, diagnosis and preventive care only.
whyNot.1: Urgent care covers immediate needs such as pain relief, not a planned course like this.
whyNot.2: Band 3 is for laboratory work such as crowns, bridges and dentures.

A.q: Which patient is NOT automatically exempt from NHS dental charges in England?
options: A woman who gave birth 6 months ago
A patient with an HC2 certificate
A.why: Age 60 or over is not, on its own, an exemption from NHS dental charges in England.

whyNot.1: Women who have had a baby in the last 12 months are exempt.
whyNot.3: An HC2 certificate gives full help with NHS dental charges.

B.q: An NHS patient needs a crown and two fillings in one course of treatment. How many NHS charges will she pay?
B.why: Patients pay one charge per course of treatment, at the highest band needed. A crown is Band 3, which also covers the fillings.

whyNot.1: NHS charges are per course of treatment, not per item.
whyNot.2: Bands are not added together; the highest band covers everything below it.
whyNot.3: There is no per-tooth charging in the NHS band system.

B.q: Which of these is included in an NHS Band 1 course of treatment?
options: A white filling on a front tooth
B.why: Band 1 covers examination, diagnosis including X-rays, preventive advice, a scale and polish if needed and preventive care.

B.q: A patient pays her practice a fixed monthly fee that covers routine check-ups, hygiene and some treatment. What is this?
B.why: A capitation plan is a monthly fee paid to the practice, often set by the patient's oral health, covering agreed routine care.

whyNot.0: NHS charges are paid per course of treatment, not monthly to the practice.
whyNot.1: Fee per item means paying separately for each treatment.
whyNot.3: An HC3 certificate gives partial help with NHS charges; it isn't a payment plan.

C.q: An NHS patient asks if she 'has to go private' for a filling on a back molar. What is the ethical response?
options: Yes, all back-tooth fillings are private
Explain the NHS option and any private ones
Recommend private, as it earns the practice more
Tell her NHS fillings are poor quality
C.why: She must be told clearly what is available on the NHS and what is private, so she can choose without pressure.

whyNot.0: A clinically necessary filling is available on the NHS; saying otherwise misleads her.
whyNot.2: Putting income before her interests breaches GDC standards.
whyNot.3: Running down NHS care to steer her towards private treatment is misleading.

C.q: Which treatment falls into NHS Band 3?
C.why: Band 3 covers laboratory-made items such as crowns, bridges and dentures.

whyNot.0: A clinically needed scale and polish is part of Band 1.
whyNot.1: Fluoride varnish is preventive care within Band 1.

C.q: During treatment the dentist finds a tooth needs a crown instead of the planned filling. What should happen?
options: Update the plan and estimate, and get consent
Do the crown and explain the cost later
Keep the original price as a goodwill gesture
Leave the tooth and say nothing
C.why: When treatment changes, the patient needs an updated plan and cost estimate and must agree before it goes ahead.

whyNot.1: Changing treatment and cost without agreement means consent isn't valid.
whyNot.2: The issue isn't price; the patient must understand and agree to the change.
whyNot.3: The patient has a right to know about a change in their treatment needs.

reteach.title: Think of the bands as nesting boxes
reteach.question: Picture three boxes that fit inside each other. If you need what's in the biggest box, do you also pay for the smaller ones?

blocks.body: The small box is Band 1: the check-up, X-rays, advice and preventive care. Band 2 is a bigger box that holds Band 1 plus fillings, root canals and extractions. Band 3 is the biggest box, holding everything plus lab-made items like crowns, bridges and dentures. A course of treatment is charged once, at the biggest box needed, so a crown plus two fillings is one Band 3 charge. Exempt patients pay nothing, whichever box they need.

blocks.text: Don't add bands together. Band 2 plus Band 3 work in the same course is just one Band 3 charge.

explain.body: Band 1: examination, diagnosis, X-rays, advice, scale and polish if needed, preventive care. Band 2: Band 1 plus fillings, root canal treatment and extractions. Band 3: Bands 1 and 2 plus crowns, bridges and dentures. Urgent care is charged at the Band 1 rate.

test.q: Which treatment is in NHS Band 2?
test.why: Fillings are Band 2 treatments, along with root canal treatment and extractions.

explain.body: In England, patients are exempt if they are under 18, under 19 in qualifying full-time education, pregnant or had a baby in the last 12 months, on qualifying benefits, or hold an HC2. HC3 gives partial help. Being over 60 is not an exemption.

rows.label: Pregnant or baby in last 12 months

test.q: A pregnant patient asks about NHS dental charges. What applies?
options: She pays a reduced Band 1 rate
She is exempt from NHS charges
She is exempt only from Band 3
She pays until her baby is born
test.why: Pregnant women, and those who have had a baby in the last 12 months, are exempt from NHS dental charges.

whyNot.0: There is no reduced rate; she is fully exempt.
whyNot.3: The exemption applies during pregnancy and for 12 months after the birth.

explain.body: Private care can be paid per item, through a capitation or maintenance plan, or via insurance. Patients must get a written plan and costs, know what is NHS and what is private, and never be pressured or misled.

test.q: Which is an example of unethical upselling?
options: Giving a written estimate before treatment
Explaining both NHS and private options
Saying needed care is only available privately
Offering time to think before deciding
test.why: Implying clinically necessary treatment isn't available on the NHS misleads the patient and puts profit before their interests.

whyNot.0: A written estimate is required good practice.
whyNot.1: Explaining all options supports informed choice.
whyNot.3: Giving time to decide avoids pressure and is good practice.
